options.content: Making single products to meet each customer's own needs
options.rationale: Correct: each job is different.

options.content: Making identical products continuously on a production line
options.rationale: That describes flow production.

options.content: Making a limited quantity of one product, then switching
options.rationale: That describes batch production.

options.content: Buying finished goods and reselling them to customers
options.rationale: That is trading, not production.

explanation: Job production makes one-off items to individual requirements.

stem: Which product is **most** likely to be made by flow production?

options.content: Bottled soft drinks
options.rationale: Correct: a standardised product in very large quantities.

options.content: A made-to-measure wedding dress
options.rationale: Made to one customer's measurements: job production.

options.content: A carved wooden door for one house
options.rationale: A one-off item: job production.

options.content: Three types of cake in a small bakery
options.rationale: Small quantities of several products: batch production.

explanation: Flow production suits standardised products with high, steady demand.

stem: A clothing factory makes 600 school shirts in size 30, then resets its machines to make 600 in size 32. Which method is this?

options.content: Job production
options.rationale: Job production makes individual items to order.

options.content: Flow production
options.rationale: Flow production makes one product continuously without stopping.

options.content: Batch production
options.rationale: Correct: a limited quantity of one product, then a change.

options.content: Division of labour
options.rationale: This is specialisation of workers, not a production method.

explanation: Making a batch and then switching to another product is batch production.

stem: Which is a disadvantage of flow production?

options.content: The cost per unit is higher than in job production
options.rationale: Flow has the lowest cost per unit.

options.content: Each product can be changed to suit one customer
options.rationale: Flow products are standardised; this is not a disadvantage of flow.

options.content: Raw materials cannot be bought in bulk
options.rationale: Flow production buys in bulk.

options.content: A breakdown at one stage can stop the whole line
options.rationale: Correct: each stage depends on the one before.

explanation: Flow production lines are interdependent; one fault halts everything.

stem: Which is an advantage of job production?

options.content: It has the lowest cost per unit of any method
options.rationale: Job production has the highest cost per unit.

options.content: It produces very large quantities of goods quickly
options.rationale: Job production is slow.

options.content: Varied, skilled work often motivates the workers
options.rationale: Correct: each job is different and challenging.

options.content: It needs no skilled or experienced workers at all
options.rationale: Job production usually needs highly skilled workers.

explanation: Job production gives unique products, high prices and varied work, but at high cost.

stem: Why does batch production often lead to higher inventory costs than flow production?

options.content: Batch production uses no machinery at all
options.rationale: Batch production uses machines that can be reset.

options.content: Finished goods and materials are stored between batches
options.rationale: Correct: stock is held until the next batch or sale.

options.content: Each batch is made for a single named customer
options.rationale: That would be job production.

options.content: Batch production makes only one product forever on each line
options.rationale: Batch production switches between products.

explanation: Each product is made only some of the time, so stocks must be held to meet demand in between.
hints: What happens to demand for a product while a different batch is being made?

stem: A new business makes steel security gates to fit each customer's doorway. Which method should it use?

options.content: Flow production
options.rationale: Flow production needs a standardised product and high demand.

options.content: Batch production
options.rationale: Each gate is different, so identical batches are not possible.

options.content: Mass production
options.rationale: Mass production is another name for flow, unsuitable here.

options.content: Job production
options.rationale: Correct: every gate is made to different measurements.

explanation: Made-to-measure items with small demand suit job production.

stem: A soap maker plans to change from batch to flow production. Which condition is **most** important for this to succeed?

options.content: Customers wanting soap made to their own recipe
options.rationale: That would suit job production.

options.content: High and steady demand for one standard type of soap
options.rationale: Correct: a line must run continuously to cover its cost.

options.content: A shortage of money to spend on new machinery
options.rationale: Flow production needs a lot of capital.

options.content: Frequent changes in the shape and colour of soap
options.rationale: Flow production suits standardised products.

explanation: Flow production's high set-up cost is only covered by large, continuous sales.
hints: What does a production line need in order to keep running?

stem: Flow production usually has the lowest cost per unit of the three methods.
explanation: True. Specialist machines, bulk buying and huge output spread costs thinly.

stem: A large business can only use one method of production.
explanation: False. Many businesses use flow for best-sellers and batch or job for other products.

stem: A furniture workshop changes to batch production of stools. Each month fixed costs are US\$4,800, the variable cost is US\$3.20 per stool and it makes 1,500 stools. Calculate the average cost per stool.
Explain **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of batch production for a bakery.

points.description: Advantage, e.g. variety of breads and cakes / flexible to demand (1)
Explained: bakery can switch to more cakes before holidays / customers have choice (1)
Disadvantage, e.g. time lost cleaning and resetting mixers and ovens between batches (1)
Explained: no output while changing over, raising cost per loaf / stock of each product held (1)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Batch production lets the bakery make several types of bread and cake, so customers have a choice and it can bake more cakes before holidays. However, mixers and ovens must be cleaned and reset between batches, and nothing is produced during this time, so the cost of each loaf rises.

explanation: Batch gives variety and flexibility but loses time between batches.
hints: Think about changing from one product to another.

stem: A Mutare dressmaker who makes clothes to order has been asked by a chain store to supply 3,000 identical school dresses each term. Recommend whether she should change from job production to batch production. Justify your answer.

points.description: Batch: lower cost per dress, so she can offer the chain store a competitive price (1)
Large regular order makes batch production worthwhile (1)
Problems: needs machines, cutting tables, semi-skilled staff and storage; finance needed (1)
May lose her made-to-order customers / work becomes repetitive (1)
Could combine: batch for school dresses, job for private customers (1)
Justified recommendation (1)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Batch production would allow her to cut and sew dresses in sizes, many at a time, so the cost per dress falls and she can offer the chain store a low price. A regular order of 3,000 dresses a term is large enough to justify buying extra machines and hiring machinists. However, she would need finance, space to store fabric and finished dresses, and staff, and the work is repetitive. I recommend she uses batch production for the school dresses while keeping a small job-production section for her private customers, so she does not lose her existing income.

explanation: Volume and standardisation favour batch; finance, space and existing customers must be considered.
hints: Consider the size and nature of the new order.

stem:
Tatenda makes leather shoes in Bulawayo by job production. He is thinking of changing to batch production of school shoes in standard sizes. He has estimated the figures below. School shoes would sell for US\$55 a pair; made-to-measure shoes sell for US\$120.

| Method | Pairs of shoes a week | Cost per pair (US\$) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Job (made to measure) | 12 | 85.00 |
| Batch (standard sizes) | 200 | 41.00 |

parts.label: (a)

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the weekly profit from batch production, assuming all pairs are sold.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the cost per pair is lower in batch production.

points.description: Machines/templates used for many identical pairs; less skilled time per pair (1)
Materials bought in bulk / costs spread over more output (1)

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Recommend whether Tatenda should change to batch production. Justify your answer.

points.description: Profit rises from US\$420 to US\$2,800 a week if all are sold (1)
But demand for 200 pairs a week is uncertain; school demand is seasonal (1)
Needs finance for machines, storage of stock (1)
Loses unique, high-price product and skilled job satisfaction (1)
Could keep job production alongside (1)

hints: Profit per pair = price − cost per pair.

stem: Masvingo Mills Ltd grinds maize meal using batch production, making 10 kg bags and 25 kg bags on the same machines. Demand for the 10 kg bag is high and steady across the year. The directors are considering a new flow production line just for 10 kg bags.

Explained: meets high, steady demand; easier quality checks (1)
